description: Mole Negro Oaxacan is a culinary masterpiece, a rich and complex black mole sauce originating from Oaxaca, Mexico. Its deep, smoky flavor comes from a blend of multiple chiles, spices, nuts, and a touch of chocolate, creating an unforgettable gastronomic experience. This traditional dish is often served with chicken or turkey, perfect for a special dinner.

ingredients.notes: shredded or in pieces, for serving

instructions.title: Prepare the Chiles
instructions.text: Heat a dry comal or skillet over medium heat. Toast the mulato, pasilla, and ancho chiles for 1-2 minutes per side until fragrant, being careful not to burn them. Remove from heat, place in a bowl, cover with hot water, and let them rehydrate for 20-30 minutes until soft. Drain and set aside.

instructions.title: Roast Vegetables and Aromatics
instructions.text: On the same comal, roast the tomatillos, tomatoes, onion, and garlic until softened and slightly charred. This will enhance their flavor and add depth to the mole.

instructions.title: Toast Nuts and Spices
instructions.text: In a small dry skillet, toast the almonds, pecans, and sesame seeds separately until golden and fragrant. Be careful as sesame seeds toast quickly. In the same skillet, toast the cinnamon stick, cloves, peppercorns, oregano, and thyme for about 30 seconds until aromatic.

instructions.title: Sauté Plantain and Raisins
instructions.text: In a separate pan with a little oil, lightly fry the sliced plantain until golden. Add the raisins and cook for another minute, just until plump. This adds a touch of sweetness.

instructions.title: Blend the Mole Base
instructions.text: Combine the rehydrated chiles, roasted vegetables, toasted nuts, spices, fried plantain, and raisins in a blender. Add 1 cup of chicken broth and blend until a very smooth paste forms. You may need to do this in batches, adding more broth as needed to achieve a thick, pourable consistency. Strain if desired for an even smoother texture.

instructions.title: Cook the Mole
instructions.text: In a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, heat the lard or vegetable oil over medium heat. Carefully pour in the blended mole paste. Cook, stirring constantly, for at least 20-30 minutes. This is crucial for developing the deep flavors and darkening the mole. The mole will splatter, so use a splatter screen or cook carefully.

instructions.title: Simmer and Finish
instructions.text: Gradually stir in the remaining 3 cups of chicken broth. Bring to a simmer, then reduce heat to low, cover, and cook for another 30 minutes, stirring occasionally. The mole should thicken and darken further. Stir in the chopped chocolate until fully melted and incorporated. Season with salt to taste.

instructions.title: Serve
instructions.text: Add the cooked chicken or turkey pieces to the mole and simmer for 5-10 minutes to heat through. Serve hot with rice, warm tortillas, and a sprinkle of sesame seeds for garnish. Enjoy this taste of Oaxaca!

tips: For a truly authentic Mole Negro, consider using Mexican chocolate, which often contains cinnamon and a hint of spice, adding another layer of traditional flavor.

The toasting of chiles, nuts, and spices is absolutely critical for developing the deep, complex flavors of the mole. Do not skip this step, but be careful not to burn them as it will make the mole bitter.
Mole Negro can be made ahead of time. In fact, its flavors often deepen and improve overnight. Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or freeze for longer storage.
article:
Embark on a culinary journey to the heart of Oaxaca, Mexico, where flavors dance and traditions thrive. Among its many gastronomic treasures, one dish stands supreme: Mole Negro Oaxacan. This isn't just a sauce; it's a profound culinary statement, a symphony of ingredients meticulously combined to create an unforgettable experience. Often considered the queen of moles, Oaxacan Black Mole is renowned for its deep, complex flavor profile, dark, velvety texture, and the sheer effort involved in its creation. It’s a dish steeped in history, celebrated at festivals, weddings, and family gatherings, representing the rich tapestry of Mexican culture. If you're looking to explore authentic Mexican dinner recipes that tell a story, preparing Mole Negro Oaxacan is an adventure well worth taking.

## What is Mole Negro Oaxacan?

Mole Negro Oaxacan is the most famous and arguably the most complex of Oaxaca's "seven moles," each distinguished by its unique blend of chiles and spices. The term "mole" itself derives from the Nahuatl word "mōlli," meaning "sauce" or "concoction," and it refers to a rich, often thick sauce made from a variety of ingredients, typically including chiles, spices, nuts, seeds, and often chocolate. "Negro," meaning "black," refers to the sauce's characteristic dark hue, which comes from the careful toasting and roasting of several types of dried chiles, along with other darkening agents like Mexican chocolate and black sesame seeds.

What sets Mole Negro Oaxacan apart is its extraordinary depth of flavor. It masterfully balances smoky, earthy notes from charred chiles with hints of sweetness from fruits, chocolate, and piloncillo (unrefined brown sugar), a subtle bitterness, and a warmth from an extensive list of spices. It’s a dish that requires patience and dedication, often involving dozens of ingredients and multiple steps, but the result is a sauce that is both ancient and eternally satisfying, a true masterpiece of Mexican dinner recipes.

## Ingredients for Authentic Mole Negro

The magic of Mole Negro Oaxacan lies in its vast and varied ingredient list. While specific ratios can differ from family to family, certain components are non-negotiable for an authentic flavor profile. Preparing this dish is less about following a rigid recipe and more about understanding the role each ingredient plays.

The foundation of any good mole is its chiles. For Mole Negro, you'll typically find a combination of dried chiles such as Mulato, Pasilla, Ancho, and sometimes Chipotle. These chiles are carefully toasted, rehydrated, and often deseeded, contributing not just heat, but also smoky, fruity, and earthy undertones, and, crucially, the deep black color.

Next come the spices, a veritable aromatic orchestra. Cinnamon sticks, cloves, black peppercorns, cumin seeds, anise seeds, thyme, marjoram, and Mexican oregano are commonly used, each toasted to release its full fragrance before being ground.

To achieve its signature body and texture, mole relies on an array of thickeners and enriching agents. These often include toasted nuts like almonds and peanuts, seeds such as sesame and pumpkin seeds, and sometimes even a few stale tortillas or a piece of bread, which also help absorb and distribute flavors. Plantains or ripe bananas are often added for sweetness and a smooth consistency.

Aromatics like white onion, garlic, tomatoes, and tomatillos are roasted or fried to develop sweetness and acidity, providing a fresh counterpoint to the richness. Sweetness is further enhanced by raisins or prunes, and crucially, Mexican chocolate. Unlike regular eating chocolate, Mexican chocolate is typically less sweet, often grainy, and flavored with cinnamon, which is vital for the mole’s distinctive taste. A touch of piloncillo or brown sugar balances the bitterness of the chiles and chocolate.

Finally, a good quality chicken or turkey broth forms the liquid base, bringing all these disparate elements together into a cohesive sauce. A little lard or vegetable oil is essential for frying the ingredients and sautéing the finished mole paste, developing its deep flavor.

## Step-by-Step Guide to Making Oaxacan Black Mole

Making Mole Negro Oaxacan is a labor of love, a multi-stage process that rewards patience with unparalleled flavor. While a full recipe would include precise measurements, here's an overview of the traditional steps:

1.  **Prepare the Chiles:** Begin by toasting the dried chiles on a comal or dry skillet until fragrant, being careful not to burn them. Rehydrate them in hot water until soft, then deseed and devein.
2.  **Toast Nuts and Spices:** Separately toast the nuts (almonds, peanuts), seeds (sesame, pumpkin), and whole spices (cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, cumin) until aromatic.
3.  **Fry Aromatics and Thickeners:** In a little lard or oil, fry the onion, garlic, tomatoes, tomatillos, plantains, and any bread or tortillas until softened and slightly caramelized.
4.  **Blend in Batches:** Combine the rehydrated chiles, toasted nuts, seeds, spices, and fried aromatics with some of the broth. Blend thoroughly until very smooth. This step often requires multiple blending sessions. For an exceptionally smooth mole, strain the blended mixture through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing out all the liquid and discarding the solids. This is perhaps the most laborious but critical step for an authentic texture.
5.  **Cook the Mole:** Heat a generous amount of lard or oil in a large, heavy-bottomed pot. Add the strained mole paste and cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for at least 30-60 minutes. This slow frying process is essential for developing the mole's deep flavor and darkening its color. It will thicken considerably.
6.  **Simmer and Season:** Gradually add more chicken or turkey broth, stirring continuously, until the mole reaches your desired consistency. Add the Mexican chocolate, piloncillo, raisins, and any other sweeteners. Continue to simmer for at least another hour, or even several hours, stirring occasionally, allowing the flavors to meld and deepen. Season generously with salt to taste. The longer it simmers, the richer it becomes.

## Tips for the Perfect Mole Negro Oaxacan

Crafting the perfect Mole Negro Oaxacan is an art, but these tips can help you achieve a truly spectacular result:

*   **Quality Ingredients are Key:** There are so many ingredients, and each contributes significantly. Seek out fresh, high-quality dried chiles and whole spices.
*   **Patience is a Virtue:** This is not a quick dish. Allow ample time for toasting, blending, and especially for the long simmering process. Rushing will compromise the depth of flavor.
*   **Don't Burn the Chiles:** When toasting chiles, a fine line exists between toasted and burnt. Burnt chiles will impart a bitter flavor to your mole. Toast them just until fragrant and slightly puffed.
*   **Strain, Strain, Strain:** While optional for some moles, straining is highly recommended for Mole Negro. It creates that signature silky-smooth texture that distinguishes it.
*   **Taste and Adjust:** As you simmer, taste frequently. The balance of sweet, spicy, smoky, and earthy notes is delicate. Adjust salt, sugar, or even a touch of acidity (like a splash of lime juice) if needed.
*   **Make Ahead:** Mole is one of those dishes that tastes even better the next day. The flavors have more time to meld and deepen, making it an excellent option for entertaining.

## Serving Suggestions for Black Mole

Traditionally, Mole Negro Oaxacan is served with poultry. Shredded chicken or turkey pieces are gently simmered in the finished mole sauce, allowing the meat to absorb its rich flavors. It's almost always accompanied by fluffy white rice, which helps to soak up every last drop of the luscious sauce, and warm corn tortillas for scooping.

Beyond this classic pairing, black mole is incredibly versatile. It can be used to make enmoladas (tortillas dipped in mole and filled with cheese or chicken), tamales, or even as a sauce for pork or beef. Garnish your mole dish with a sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds, finely chopped white onion, or fresh cilantro for added texture and visual appeal. For a truly authentic experience, serve it with a side of refried beans or a simple salad.

## Variations and Substitutions

While the traditional recipe for Mole Negro Oaxacan is highly revered, home cooks often make subtle adjustments based on ingredient availability or personal preference.

*   **Chiles:** While the core chiles (Mulato, Pasilla, Ancho) are essential, some might add a different smoky chile like Morita for an extra kick, or adjust the ratios based on desired heat level.
*   **Nuts and Seeds:** If certain nuts or seeds are unavailable, you can experiment with others like pecans or cashews, though this will slightly alter the flavor profile. Almonds and sesame seeds are particularly characteristic.
*   **Sweeteners:** Piloncillo is ideal, but dark brown sugar can be used as a substitute.
*   **Chocolate:** Authentic Mexican chocolate is highly recommended. If unavailable, a high-quality dark chocolate (70% cocoa or higher) with a pinch of cinnamon can be used, but it won't have the same earthy undertones.
*   **Vegetarian/Vegan Mole:** For a plant-based version, simply substitute chicken or turkey broth with a rich vegetable broth. Serve the Mole Negro Oaxacan over roasted vegetables like sweet potatoes or cauliflower, or with plant-based protein like mushrooms or seitan.

Mole Negro Oaxacan is more than just a meal; it's a culinary legacy. Its creation is a meditative act, a connection to generations of Mexican cooks who have perfected this intricate sauce. While it demands time and effort, the reward is an unparalleled depth of flavor that will transport your taste buds straight to the heart of Oaxaca. Take the plunge, embrace the process, and discover the magic of this truly iconic Mexican dinner recipe.
